💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France.
  • Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried.
  • It has been revealed that hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”.

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” says Dakota, who’s in Fresh York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value costar Stellan Skarsgård. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”.

It has been revealed that hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”.

According to recent reports, now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” states Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”.

Sources indicate that the Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”.

Sources indicate that dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” notes Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”.

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, claims she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”.

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complementary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”.

Industry observers note that morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”.

According to recent reports, of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who, after reading the 2015 historical novel, told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne reveals her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” says Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”.

Recent findings suggest that although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”.

Their director states because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them, and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”.

The Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” claims Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”.

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” indicates Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”.

But they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” claims Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”.

Edmund Donovan and Elle Fanning.

Industry observers note that “It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”.

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar-winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”.

Recent findings suggest that morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”.

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her costars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn’t grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”.

Industry observers note that hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s vital historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”.

It wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position, and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”.

Industry observers note that “Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew, and they were grinning from ear to ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”.

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”.

According to recent reports, hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”.

According to recent reports, nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”.

Recent findings suggest that to hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets, and I’ve seen her work,” claims Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”.

According to recent reports, “But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she notes, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I'm a proud theater kid, one who is still acting and producing to this day in the community theater space.
  • While Club Kid is my favorite movie of the year (so far), Elsinore is another LGBTQ+ story that I feel privileged to have seen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actor Andrew Scott is synonymous with playing Hot Priest in Fleabag (streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription), but he's a versatile star of the screen and stage. Those two worlds combine in the new LGBTQ+ movie Elsinore, directed by Simone Stone. The biographical drama film tells the story of late actor Ian Charleson, who performed the title role of Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly struggling with AIDS in the midst of the AIDS crisis. The movie is endlessly powerful, and I have so many thoughts as someone who comes from the theatre.

I'm a proud theater kid, one who is still acting and producing to this day in the community theater space. While I loved Andrew Scott's stunning performance in Elsinore and the way it honored Charleson and the countless queer folks that we lost to the AIDS crisis, I was also taken by how accurately the new film portrayed what it's like to work in theater... warts and all.

While Club Kid is my favorite movie of the year (so far), Elsinore is another LGBTQ+ story that I feel privileged to have seen. The movie tells the real-life story of Ian Charleson struggling with AIDS while also preparing to play the behemoth role of Hamlet at the National Theatre. It's a truly gut-wrenching story, told expertly through the film's 111-minute runtime. Throughout the movie, I was shook by how seen I felt by the way it portrayed working on a theater production.

To start, there was the almost neurotic way that Ian is shown preparing to play the titular character Hamlet. We see him working long hours in the sparse rehearsal room, where experimentation and heeding notes from director Richard Eyre transformed his performance from a piece of marble into a detailed statue. While stage actors make this look easy, there is way more work than casual audiences might grasp from their seat in the house.

Then there was the process of line memorization. Ian is shown drilling lines pretty much non-stop throughout Elsinore, including when he's getting treatments and even while recovering after being hospitalized. This rings so true to me; if I'm in a dialogue-heavy play, I function in the same way. For instance, when I played Prior Walter in Tony Kushner's Angels in America, I couldn't stop drilling my lines. That includes testing myself with flashcards, as well as repeating my monologues every time I was in the shower and/or driving in the car.

Much like Ian in Elsinore, getting those lines ingrained in my head allows for more freedom and expression during performances, rather than searching for what comes next in my head.

Then there's the sense of community that's shown in the latest movie. While Ian spends most of the movie hiding his diagnosis, he eventually tells them the truth before opening night. He expected judgment, but his colleagues rapidly accept him and offer support for his performance. This feels very true to the experience of being in the theater; weird chosen families often form with each production. I've seen ensembles rally around people struggling with grief, miscarriages, election results and more.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Overall, it really felt like Elsinore was created by folks who knew and love what it means to work in the theater. Obviously this isn't the point of the movie per se, but it's one of many reasons why I thought it was so incredible.

Sources indicate that elsinore is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. Word to the wise: bring your tissues.

Sources indicate that corey was born and raised in New Jersey. Graduated with degrees theater and literature from Ramapo College of New Jersey. After working in administrative theater for a year in New York, he started as the Weekend Editor at CinemaBlend. He's since been able to work himself up to reviews, phoners, and press junkets-- and is now able to appear on camera with some of his favorite actors... just not as he would have predicted as a kid. He's particularly proud of covering horror franchises like Scream and Halloween, as well as movie musicals like West Side Story. Favorite interviews include Steven Spielberg, Spike Lee, Jamie Lee Curtis, and more.

Jessica Simpson has parted ways with her signature blonde tresses in favor of a darker — and more winter-like — shade.

According to recent reports, “They say blondes have more fun,” celebrity hairstylist Ken Paves wrote via his Instagram Stories on Friday, November 20, alongside a selfie featuring Simpson, 46. “She says brunettes have fun and then some.”.

Simpson, who reposted the snap onto her account, dressed casually in all-black. As for her glam, the singer’s newly darkened mane was styled in loose, face-framing waves.

While Simpson is often synonymous with her honey-colored hair, she made a major statement late last year when she went brunette.

Industry observers note that “It took a few hours to color because we kept making it darker and darker,” her colorist Rita Hazan told People in December 2025. “I didn’t want to go too dark at once, so we gradually increased the hue to ensure that we got the most perfect tone.”.

Industry observers note that she continued, “For years we kept different variations of either blonde or very blonde. Just recently I took her dirty blonde, and the shade continues to get deeper and more brunette.”.

According to Hazan, Simpson’s darker ‘do even matched her “very moody” music return. The performer released her long-awaited follow-up EP, Nashville Canyon Part 1, earlier that year.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that âThere is so much to do in Leonida, and so much to discover, that we hope players get to the point where they stop thinking in tasks, completion percentages, online guides and rather let the game unfold in front of them,” VP of design Stephen Donkin said in a packet of studio development notes shared with press.
  • According to recent reports, donkin’s first Rockstar credit was as a QA tester on GTA 5, and his advice for GTA 6 players echoed the feelings of some of the studio’s other developers when it comes to taking in the immersive beauty and emergent nuance of the newly introduced entry’s complex world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar Games.

Tens of millions of people are playing Grand Theft Auto 6 right now. What’s the best way to experience Rockstar’s latest open-world epic? According to one of the developers themselves, you should play it with as little anxiety around checklists and online noise as possible.

Recent findings suggest that âThere is so much to do in Leonida, and so much to discover, that we hope players get to the point where they stop thinking in tasks, completion percentages, online guides and rather let the game unfold in front of them,” VP of design Stephen Donkin said in a packet of studio development notes shared with press. “When you play the game and take your time with it, playing at the pace it asks you to, it can really unfold in front of you in a way that can feel almost infinite at a macro level, but each individual encounter still feels hand-crafted and with a human behind it.

According to recent reports, donkin’s first Rockstar credit was as a QA tester on GTA 5, and his advice for GTA 6 players echoed the feelings of some of the studio’s other developers when it comes to taking in the immersive beauty and emergent nuance of the newly introduced entry’s complex world. âThere are clearly tons of high-stakes, high-energy, fast-paced moments and thrills and laughs along the way, but there are also quiet, meditative experiences and adventures to be had that offer a fully different feeling,” stated senior design director Ghyan Koehne. “If I had to be held to a single feeling, Iâd say âwonder.â We want players to be constantly presented with a feeling of wonderâwe hope everyone feels a mixture of emotions.â.

It’s a stark contrast to how GTA lives in the popular imagination of most people, which is as a chaos sim full of drugs, sex, and violent crime. GTA 6 has those things, but they are far less domineering parts of the experience this time around. It’s also completely divorced from how some people often experience modern video games, which is heavily augmented by a second-screen experience full of achievement guides, TikTok memes, and social media rage-bait.

People should play GTA 6 however they want, but I’d encourage them to take at least a few hours to experience the game in the dark with headphones on and as little knowledge as possible of what awaits them and how the whole thing works, their phones and laptops safely tucked away in a different room. Former Kotaku editor Kirk Hamilton was famous for telling people to turn off parts of the onscreen UI to make the experience more immersive and make it feel less like a chore list. Every significant latest open-world game that came out there would be a post about turning off the minimap.

In a recent development, I’ve never been able to play games that way. I’m too fidgety and squirrely for that kind of thing. But I always try to spend at least a couple hours in that headspace, treating what’s in front of me more as something worth experiencing for its own sake than just as a maze to speedrun through as efficiently as possible in exchange for in-game rewards, entertaining setpieces, and satisfying emotional climaxes. That’s an increasingly alien way of approaching anything in our algorithmically optimized world, but GTA 6 offers as good a reason as any to try it.

“If players can let go and submit to becoming immersed in the world of Leonida, and just follow their nose as they play, they will feel the Leonida I have felt,” Donkin stated, “And thatâs all we could ask for.â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tasha Suri, author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy and several other books, will be writing Baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart, the official BG3books website has confirmed. Another prequel to Larian's videogame, this one focuses on Shadowheart's time as a priestess in the Church of Shar, and is about a murder mystery.

Recent findings suggest that "When a member of their order is killed in the Upper City," the blurb goes, "Shadowheart and her so-called allies are called to investigate. She trusts none of them: not Mirie, the ambitious Griefguard; not Caldan, the cynical propagandist; and certainly not Nocturne, the charming quartermistress, who claims to have only Shadowheart’s best interests in mind.".

Sources indicate that mirie and Nocturne are both characters you can meet in Baldur's Gate 3, while Caldan Darkwood is mentioned in a note you can find. Nocturne in particular has a close relationship with Shadowheart, which could be interesting to see developed. "Torn between the familiar comforts of the dark and the thrill of upcoming desire," the blurb continues, "she must solve the mystery to prove her devotion… or be cast into the light.".

Which sounds fine and dandy, but it'll have an uphill battle with the Baldur's Gate 3 fandom, who've been vocally critical of the Astarion novel for its lightness of tone—especially given his traumatic backstory—and apparently mischaracterizing Astarion and his sire, Cazador, as well as being inaccurate to the lore.

I haven't read the Astarion book, but I did read the original Baldur's Gate novels, which were terrible. So were almost all the D&D books I read in a youthful post-Tolkien haze where I'd put up with anything that had wizards in it. My expectations are pretty low, but I do like to slip a trashy fantasy novel between heavier reads as a palate-cleanser so maybe I'll try this one some day.

Recent findings suggest that baldur's Gate 3: Shadowheart will be out in a 304-page hardcover edition and in ebook form on June 8, as well as a 10-hour audiobook. The Astarion audiobook was read by Astarion performer Neil Newbon, we'll have to wait and see if Jennifer English reads the Shadowheart book.

If the series continues I could see a Wyll prequel being interesting, since he gets a bit short-changed in the videogame, though I wouldn't expect it to sell as well as novels about the more popular companions.

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months.
  • According to recent reports, but it was not a human therapist.
  • In Sherry Turkle’s fresh book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what would happen if she spilled the beans. Was she worried about permanently losing face? About being publicly labeled as “mentally ill”? Was she concerned by the thought of this information harming those who loved her? And she would have been pushed on what Rubicon had been crossed and why it was one from which she believed she could not return.

According to recent reports, but it was not a human therapist. Sophie died in February of last year.

In Sherry Turkle’s fresh book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being. She is not anti-AI but strongly cautions against relationships with machines. Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, spoke to me mid-book tour, her recent weeks a blur of speaking gigs and bookstore events, with more ahead of her. Not all event attendees are keen on her message.

According to recent reports, “People love their chatbots. They’re in deep. They’re talking to them about everything—about their marriages and how to talk to their husbands and wives; whether, developmentally, their children are at the right place. They talk about their anxiety, their medical conditions,” Turkle tells Vanity Fair. “During this tour, you wouldn’t believe the number of people who will just stand up at a bookstore and say, ‘I think that it loves me more than anything has loved me. Who are you, Debbie Downer?’ [They don’t like] somebody who comes in and notes, ‘Look, how can we keep it in its lane?’”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: I think you’re saying [our relationship with chatbots] is bad for us.

Sherry Turkle: It’s bad for us when it talks in the first person. We are biologically wired to respond to something that speaks to us in the first person as though it is a person. I mean, all those years of evolution—the only thing we came upon in the wild that spoke to us in the first person was another person.

In a recent development, if generative AI wants to discover latest drugs for Parkinson’s or work out which cancer therapies statistically are the most helpful, there are so many things to work on. Why does it have to work on relationships, love, and being a best friend, lover, mother, or therapist?

What if the sycophancy could be dialed back?

It’s inauthentic; it’s not a relationship, so anything you need a relationship for, it’s just not equipped. I really feel very strongly about this. I have had this conversation with members of the MIT community, and I basically say to them, “The better you make an AI chatbot, the worse it is.” You dial back the sycophancy so it sounds more like a reasonable person, and people are going to be more smitten and convinced they’re in a relationship. At least the sycophancy reminds you that, God, this is weird.

To become a therapist, I had to study for years and do internships and more internships and then have hundreds of supervised patient hours. I mean, I forget all the things I needed to do before I was allowed to see a patient alone in a room. Now it’s just allowed to give therapy?

Industry observers note that I’ve spent a lot of time talking to public health folks about what best practices would look like and whether there’s a way to Trojan horse in real care. Would you be more sanguine about it if the world of therapy came together with the major AI companies and provided them with therapy bots and training data that were paradigmatically appropriate to their therapy styles?

It has been revealed that so you’re asking, would I be happy if the deception was smoother? This technology is a marvel and we can use it for all kinds of things, so it’s not an anti-technology position to say that the fact that this technology can simulate these different things doesn’t mean that it is those things. It’s a statement of how far we are in the culture of simulation that pretending to be the thing and being the thing have started to feel like the same thing.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve written about the effects of robots and machines on humans for decades. The tone of this book seems darker to me.

Recent findings suggest that by 2015, I had identified social media as problematic for teenagers. [My] book [Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age] is about why we would rather text than talk, why people have this feeling of vulnerability, so they would rather do anything than have a face-to-face conversation. By 2015, I had genuine concerns.

In a recent development, and this book, I have a totally different tone. I see something ultimately very dangerous being normalized, and I didn’t feel that way in previous books.

It has been revealed that I want people to say this is the book of a really worried and concerned researcher, because I see a completely different profile for how people are using AI. I see that people feel disappointed by their families and their friends. It doesn’t make sense to me that we’re so willing to replace ourselves with something that isn’t human. Why is my position the romantic, pie-in-the-sky, dreamy position, and somebody who says, “Well, let’s just replace the people with chatbots and let’s move this party along”—why is that common sense? Why is that progressive? That seems to me to be the most regressive and most dystopian position.

You know, human beings are dedicated to keeping each other alive and wanting each other to thrive, and a chatbot just fails that basic test.

You’ve remarked no AI chatbots for kids under 18. What about our other vulnerable populations, people who are mentally unwell, or the 48 million Americans who are at the moment depressed? Do they deserve any kind of special protection from chatbots? And how much can you litigate? Do you feel like you’re the Ralph Nader of AI chatbots?

[Laughs] Yes, I am. When you stand back and look at what Ralph Nader managed to get Americans to do, to see cars as potential instruments that pointed at our vulnerability, and to ask how we could protect ourselves—there turned out to be 25 possible things that needed to be mandated for cars, then there were 30, and then there were 40. But we could get people to agree on 10, and those became part of building a car and really constrained our behavior around cars. Using the example of cars, and of smoking, when we decide that we’re vulnerable and we want to protect ourselves, we rise to the occasion.

According to recent reports, I recently heard a clip of the psychologist Orna Guralnik discussing how annoying “otherness” is in a relationship and the inherent friction of sharing your life with a separate person whose habits, values, and mind are distinct from your own. It made me wonder if, in a way, an AI chatbot is less of an “other” than a loved one.

Recent findings suggest that I think this is a very profound point, actually. So you have the illusion of a relationship without the demands of intimacy, without the demands of having to deal with another. There’s a kind of narcissistic loop that you get into. The point is, it’s not good.

It has been revealed that I talk about how you judge whether something is good for you. One litmus test is whether it increases the quality, resiliency, and richness of your inner life. That’s a way that human beings have judged relationships.

So much has been written about the epidemic of loneliness—isn’t a reasonable application for AI chatbots companionship for shut-ins and the elderly?

It has been revealed that you know, I’m never anywhere where somebody doesn’t say, “I can’t believe that you don’t want to give chatbots to old lonely people.” And I say, “Well, how about we don’t close senior centers, and we don’t close parks, and we don’t cancel Meals on Wheels? What about social infrastructure?”.

In a recent development, I’ve been on this beat for years and years, and I, too, could write a heartwarming story of an AI chatbot with a lonely old person. But you know what? A lot of them are not isolated in cabins or on islands; a lot of them just could use a friend.

Social media companies and AI companies are not saying, “Look, we’re introducing something that takes you to your screen, but we’re going to balance that with a giant social infrastructure project to make sure that people can choose a screen, but they also have every other kind of choice to be with each other.”.

According to recent reports, given he's one of the world's biggest stars, Timothée Chalamet's life remains a topic of curiosity. Of course, as a star's fame rises, it's not unheard for them to reveal less about themselves. On that note, when Vanity Fair editor Mark Guiducci was given the task of profiling the megastar, he had a bigger task than he initially thought. The interview has now gone viral for awkward reasons, but Guiducci is defending his work and sharing a complimentary note about Chalamet.

Recent findings suggest that while Guiducci is normally an editor at the aforementioned publication rather than a writer, Chalamet still personally requested for this profile to be written by him, and that feels like a pretty tall order. Because Chalamet can’t go to many places in public due to his celebrity status, Guiducci invited the star over to his own apartment. This was apparently done in the hope that if Guiducci opened his own life up to Chalamet, he would be more willing to reveal more about himself, as the editor himself told Page Six.

However, this turned out not to be the case. Chalamet remained incredibly guarded and opted out of talking about his life. He declined to answer questions or comment on his high profile relationship with Kylie Jenner (with the latter admittedly being something he's long opted not to discuss). He did however spend a lot of time making observations about Guiducci’s home decor, which ended up becoming the centerpiece of the article. As a result, the story has gone viral due to Chalamet's evasive, awkward nature as well as the piece feeling more like it's about Guiducci’s apartment rather than Chalamet.

In a recent development, despite the criticism, the Vanity Fair editor is still defending his work and his subject. He may have not been an open book, but Guiducci still made sure to note how normal the Oscar nominee felt to be around, and despite him stocking his kitchen and fridge with anything Chalamet could potentially want to eat or drink, the actor was surprisingly very low maintenance. He noted:.

Sources indicate that he was a lovely houseguest, and a cheap date. He drank tap water. And he’s welcome back any time.

Considering Chalamet grew up in Latest York City himself and still spends a lot of time in the Significant Apple, he’s likely used to drinking New York’s tap water. Plus, I wouldn't be surprised if he had some sort of awareness that if he asked for anything specific it would end up in the article. I personally don’t doubt that Chalamet was kind, charming, and easy going, especially since the Dune star has been described as being “normal” before. It’s just hard to get a true read on a person when the person in question is aware they’re being observed.

What seems to strike people most about Chalamet's lack of commentary is how it runs in contrast to how open he seemed to be during last awards season. It was during that time that he was promoting his sports dramedy, Marty Supreme. Of course, it was also during that promotional run that he received backlash for his viral comment regarding ballet and opera. However, Chalamet was defended in some circles.

Right now, the Little Women alum is under the biggest microscope possible, and it makes sense that he would have his guard up. Maybe he’ll become less guarded as time goes on, and his status as one of the last movie stars doesn’t feel so fragile. We’ll just have to wait and see.

#85863. Virginia Feito on the Film Adaptation of Her Novel ‘Victorian Psycho’

Virginia Feito on the Film Adaptation of Her Novel ‘Victorian Psycho’

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh.
  • When I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication.
  • Industry observers note that I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh.

When I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication. Generally, making a movie is one big miracle produced by an amalgamation of thousands of other tiny miracles. But when I met Zach Wigon, I understood that this was a joyfully tenacious person who was going to make this movie if it cost him his life.

Industry observers note that I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel. Among film stars, an Irish crew, and (rumored) ticks, the adaptation of Victorian Psycho—based on my screenplay, which is based on my novel, which is based on my ego, I guess—was born. Throughout the shoot I kept a sort of pseudo diary in order to remember every surreal detail from which I still haven’t recovered. I’ve chosen to reproduce some of it here.

Director Zach Wigon and producer Lisa Kelly call me from the set on the first day of shooting (Zach and I have agreed I won’t visit the set until after the first week so the cast and crew can acclimate without me hovering over them, because I am an intense fame whore, and also, I suppose, to signal I’m not crucial enough to pull a P.L. Travers and attempt to boycott the movie).

Sources indicate that over the phone, the producer claims she can’t wait to meet in person. I tell her I’m underwhelming.

According to recent reports, they promise to send me the dailies. I spend all day waiting for the dailies. The dailies never come.

At around 9 p.m., I spiral because I don’t know whether to celebrate with Champagne or KFC. I decide to have both.

It has been revealed that I finally get the dailies. I fall in love with Maika Monroe’s character so hard it’s like I have an obsessive crush circa 2006 whose Facebook photos I’m compulsively looking at. But in this case it’s the same scene throughout five almost identical takes of Maika calling a 10-year-old boy a little idiot.

Over the phone, Zach mentions concerns about a specific scene because we don’t have the budget for that many extras. I get carried away and suggest shipping over a whole battalion of free extras from Spain because, in my head, it’s going to be me and my friends, drunk and decked out in period clothing like we’re at a cheesy bachelorette party. One friend starts making childcare arrangements and another cancels her Holter monitor appointment so she can come to the shoot. What could go wrong?

I start to realize what could go wrong.

I am informed we are probably no longer going to need the extras, and I feel a huge wave of relief as I uninvite my excited friends. I pack a suitcase for Ireland. It weighs 57 pounds.

I have a steak on the plane to Dublin at, like, 3 p.m., because when you’re flying business and somebody offers you steak, you take it.

The hotel room is wonderful, but I jokingly tell Zach over the phone that it’s on a first floor, so someone might crawl up and break in through the window and rape me, and he laughs at first but then is concerned and tells me to request a room on a higher floor, and I tell him it was a joke, but it wasn’t really.

I fill up the hotel room bathtub and call reception for a glass of red wine because I am a queen and I am queening. The glass doesn’t come, so in my anxious impatience I attempt to open a bottle of red wine sitting above the minibar. The cork crumbles because I’ve never understood how to use a corkscrew—like the compass in math class, I just faked my way through it my entire life and hoped for the best. So I call reception for another glass of red wine. They bring me all the glasses of wine and also properly uncork the bottle, and I watch Seinfeld in the bathtub while I drink red wine. I get drunk and paint my nails.

According to recent reports, I arrive on set slightly Bromazepamed. It is extremely surreal to exist in a set labeled “Mr. Pounds’s Bedroom.” I am used to living in the fictional world inside my head but not used to it becoming more real than real life itself.

Industry observers note that maika hugs me when we meet, and I swallow a sob and refrain from smelling her hair (partly because it is, in fact, a wig). Everyone on set appears so happy to meet me, I suspect a Good Bye, Lenin! situation in which I have been diagnosed with cancer and for some reason the cast and crew all know but I don’t know. This isn’t the plot of Good Bye, Lenin!, but you’ll know what I mean if you’ve seen it.

Zach asks me to read the VOs in every scene, which means I’m in the scene with Ruth Wilson, Jason Isaacs, and Maika, and I’m about to have a stroke.

Jason eats for real in every single take and has already gulped down seven sausage rolls, so if I fuck up my VO, I will kill myself.

In a recent development, suddenly experiencing fiction collectively feels very superior to experiencing it privately. This does not bode well for the rest of my career as a novelist.

It has been revealed that there is a scene in a cramped drawing room in which I must read the VO, but I’m supposed to hide from the camera, so I crawl on all fours behind an antique couch and grovel my way around the room while the boom op steps on my hands. I secretly think the boom op hates me because I’m always in his way and have an irritating habit of apologizing when he slams into me.

I start developing Irish inflections, so I say it, “I start developing Irish inflections,” but the Irish seem happy about it, so I pursue it.

Jason Isaacs starts doing card tricks between takes because Jason Isaacs is actually magic and also indefatigable. Only one thing could ever defeat Jason Isaacs, and it’s the ghost allegedly living on the third floor.

Even though Zach asked me to oversee the second unit, I don’t think anyone believes I’m actually going to do this—and between you and me, I don’t really even know what a second unit is. It doesn’t help I can’t concentrate on what we’re shooting because we’re in the middle of the woods and someone mentioned there were ticks, so I’m wrapping Sellotape around my ankles, hoping this way they won’t be able to crawl up my legs.

In a recent development, like your worst trauma, I insert myself into the movie forever via a small cameo. I literally just have to stand in a wig while I smile and nod, but I do it in such a way that I ruin every single take. “Just smile…like a normal person,” the second-unit director notes. I reason Zach can just cut me out of the movie, and I will only have wasted everybody’s time and money. There are worse things, like smiling normally but having no cameo. I cope by chewing on another Bromazepam and another chocolate bar. (Every morning I take the chocolate bar from the hotel minibar. It will invariably become an asset in the long afternoons on set, kind of like in prison or high school.).

I change hotel rooms because I have developed an intense FOMO with which I’m always fearing there is a better hotel room for the same price somewhere in the vicinity. This FOMO is also rampant on set between the different units—in the first unit, you have the cinematographer, Nico Aguilar, laughing in the sunlight, talking about color palettes, while in the second unit, we’re shooting clocks and screaming at each other because we still have 17 establishing shots to go.

It has been revealed that anyway, I change hotel rooms, and the new room is so superior to my previous room it’s like an entirely new hotel. I consider changing hotel rooms further. Perhaps I can somehow upgrade my way into a presidential suite.

It has been revealed that my parents visit the set. My dad peers over his glasses at the fake lobster cake, and when I tell him the toilets are in trailers, he sighs gravely.

Jason Isaacs convinces my dad to take up tennis again even though my dad’s not supposed to play tennis after his seven hernias. But my dad is so inspired by this actor, who is not a doctor but whose performance in The Patriot my dad can’t help but praise at least once a month, that he will immediately start playing tennis again upon his return to Spain, and whatever medical problems arise henceforth shall all be Jason Isaacs’s fault.

At the Shelbourne restaurant that night, my mom tells the sommelier how she can’t drink red wine anymore because it makes her anxious, and he kneels on the floor beside her and places a hand on his heart as if she were confiding something intimate to him like her fear of death.

Suddenly, real life feels less real than fictional life.

According to recent reports, obama is visiting Dublin and he’s booked the entire floor, so he essentially kicks me out of the Shelbourne (probably to stay in the JFK Suite next door to my room, which is disappointingly predictable), so I go to The Hoxton, because what is life if you’re not constantly changing hotel rooms? The Hoxton is really lovely, but I get OCD about the light bulbs in the room because they appear mismatched, so I ask housekeeping to change them, but they claim not to have any extra light bulbs, which sounds suspect—like, what do they do if a light bulb suddenly goes out? Do they just never replace it?

We end the shoot at 5 a.m. I am wearing a thick puffer coat and a thermal T-shirt and a furry hat, plus fur-lined boots over my Sellotaped ankles, although I wonder, If ticks can survive this temperature, they kind of deserve to live off my blood. Nobody else seems as concerned about the cold as me, but then again, most of them are Irish.

Sadly, when we wrap, we are all so exhausted everyone races to clean up and leave, and it is sort of anticlimactic. I don’t know what I was expecting, but balloons falling from the skies did flash through my mind.

Industry observers note that in the car on the way to our respective quarters, Zach and I look out the window, wide-eyed, like kidnapped children. Zach starts discussing a latest project for us. I wonder if he is a sociopath.

Industry observers note that I type this over a year later, sitting at my desk in Madrid, striving to work on my next novel. I feel empty inside knowing there is no car to pick me up and take me to set and thereby escape reality for extended periods of time, until set becomes reality and reality becomes a limbo in which you wait for said reality.

In a recent development, I am working on a novel, but also on four new scripts. I hope to return to reality someday.

But now I just find the joy in every single thing that [her daughter Kaia] does. My little girl loves to play with rocks, sticks and dirt, and it’s like I never realized how cool a rock or a leaf was. You’re just reliving your own childhood all over again.”.

Us exclusively confirmed back in June 2025 that the former Vanderpump Rules bad-girl-turned-voice-of-reason and her fiancé, Luke Broderick, were officially parents after welcoming baby girl Kaia.

It has been revealed that “She’s here, and we still can’t believe it. Luke is even hotter as a dad, and I just feel so lucky,” Doute told Us at the time. “And even though I haven’t slept or showered in two days, seeing our daughter and finally being able to hold her makes it all worth it. We’re completely overwhelmed with love and so grateful for her— our lives are already changed completely.”.

Doute later opened up to Us about life as a upcoming mom, admitting that while she felt “really lucky” and “really fortunate” she was also exhausted and still adjusting to parenthood.

In a recent development, “I’m good. I mean, I’m exhausted. The tired thing is no joke. Maybe a day and a half ago, Luke and I had this system down: We’re like, OK, she’s napping; when she gets up, the bottle, the diapers are ready, all good to go. We were like, we got this, and we high-fived,” she told Us in July 2025. “Then last night I woke up, my boobs were exploding, I’m covered in milk, she’s screaming and crying, and we’re both like, ‘Oh my God, what do we do? We’re all figuring things out together.”.

The pair’s postpartum struggles and relationship woes as new parents were heavily documented on season 3 of The Valley — a steep learning curve that was often painful for Kristen but, thanks to her daughter, one that was also healing, she told Us.

It has been revealed that she had heard mine. Years earlier, older girls at the school had told her about me. She held on to my name, and when she went to a lawyer she remembered it. By then I had married and changed it, and they found me anyway.

According to recent reports, I called Matt and asked. “Who is Melissa?” There was a pause long enough to hear him decide something, then a sigh, and then he told me he had had sex with Melissa while she was a student.

Here is what I did next, and I’d ask you to withhold judgment. I told him I would call the lawyer, find out what she had, and report back.

That’s what twenty-two years of being groomed looks like at a desk in Midtown. You don’t make a decision. The decision was made for you a long time ago, in a dorm room, and you’re simply carrying it out.

Sources indicate that I did call the lawyer. And when I heard my own voice say “I’m not ready to talk to you, I want to talk to Melissa,” I think that was the first sentence in two decades that I said entirely for myself.

Recent findings suggest that melissa called that afternoon. I don’t remember how she started. I remember what I stated before she got far.

“I’ve been waiting for your call for twenty years.”.

It has been revealed that I meant it literally. Some part of me had always known I wasn’t the only one. I just couldn’t go looking. I could only wait to be found.

Hilary Simon and Melissa Fares, photographed in Far Rockaway, New York, 2025.

Recent findings suggest that she told me her story, and I heard my own memories come out of a stranger’s mouth. He called her “Little One.” He called me “Little One.” He took her to the same hotel in Northampton. He told her he would kill himself if she ever told anyone, which is a thing he had also told me, more than once, in nearly the same words. He had made himself the center of her emotional world before he ever touched her. He had a script.

For twenty years he had me believing that what happened was singular, and that it was my fault. By the end of that call it was a pattern, and I was a data point. I was not special. It is a strange thing to grieve, not being special to the person who hurt you. I grieved it anyway.

After more than three decades teaching at that school, he resigned the same day.

Industry observers note that I arrived at Miss Hall’s, an all-girls boarding school in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in the fall of 2001. I was fourteen, homesick, and like every other girl my age, positive I was more grown up than I was.

Rutledge had been teaching history there for a decade. He was a substantial man with a booming voice, married with two daughters. He lived with his family in a school-owned house across the street from the main entrance. He used to cut the lunch line announcing himself as “Mr. Wonderful.” Girls talked about him like he was a minor deity. They also mentioned, in the breezy way teenagers mention terrible things, that he had a type.

Recent findings suggest that some evenings, he was one of the adults who did bed checks in the dorms. The others always stood in the doorway. He came in and sat on the edge of my bed.

By the next fall he was my advisor and my cross-country coach. There was no door at that school he couldn’t open. On the long drives to meets, he told me to sit next to him in the school van. He called me his copilot. The rest of the team sat behind us. He would put his hand on my upper thigh, or pull me close until our legs were touching. I watched the Berkshire hills go by and tried not to look down.

That was the first line he crossed. I was fifteen. After that he crossed them one at a time until there were none left. He kept abusing me for years after I graduated.

From the outside, those years looked like a success story.

I went to college and then law school. I became a civil defense attorney. I got married. I had a son. I was good at my job.

It has been revealed that I could find the unanswered email in ten thousand pages of discovery. The report nobody followed up on. I couldn’t open my own file.

Sources indicate that when I tell this story, people ask me some version of the same question. How did nobody notice?

In the late 1990s, years before I ever set foot on Miss Hall’s campus, a student stood up at a school meeting and said Mr. Rutledge was having sex with another student. The school suspended her for the rest of the year, barred her from graduation and made her write him an apology letter. He kept teaching.

On my graduation day, Rutledge kissed me and told me that he loved me. A classmate told a staff member, who reported it to the administration. In a memo, Rutledge admitted telling me he loved me but said “[it was] not a romantic expression.” He denied the kiss. They took his word for it. No one called me or my parents.

Hilary Simon on graduation day.

A few years later, after a family reported that he had made advances toward their daughter, the head of school at that time, Jeannie Norris, put a warning to Rutledge in writing. “This isn’t the 70s or the 80s,” she wrote. “Society has no stomach for any kind of inappropriate behavior between adults and girls or teachers and students.” She was worried about the school’s reputation, and about his. In the letter she stated the incident had “the potential for seriously damaging the School and your [Rutledge’s] reputation.” He was not fired.

Over the years that followed Rutledge was made chair of the history department and collected faculty honors. More than one person gave the school my name as a girl he had singled out. Nobody ever called me. In June 2023, I heard another alumna tried to raise concerns about him with the head of school at that time. He was still teaching nine months later, when Melissa reported him.

In August 2025 Miss Hall’s published the results of an outside investigation it had commissioned from Aleta Law. The investigators substantiated grooming and abuse by Rutledge involving at least five students. They found school leadership had been warned about him over the years and hadn’t acted. Staff members told investigators they had suspected him and kept quiet, some because they feared retaliation, others because they assumed no one in charge would listen.

It went beyond Rutledge. The investigation found that seven other Miss Hall’s employees had engaged in sexual misconduct with students, dating back to the 1940s. Eight adults across eighty plus years. That’s a culture of abuse.

Recent findings suggest that A Berkshire County grand jury has since indicted Norris on a charge of reckless endangerment of a child. She has pleaded not guilty. Another former Miss Hall’s teacher has been indicted for assault with intent to rape and indecent assault and two counts battery of a student. He has also pleaded not guilty.

I read all sixty pages of the Aleta Law report in one sitting. Nothing in it surprised me. It still knocked the air out of me to see my adolescence reduced to numbered findings.

Melissa arrived at Miss Hall’s in 2007, two years after I left.

According to recent reports, people sometimes call us friends. That’s true, but it’s a small word for it. I call her my sister survivor.

In a recent development, I wouldn’t be writing this if Melissa hadn’t gone first. She went to the school alone. In April 2024, she told her story publicly. A few weeks later, I told mine. Then other women came forward. They mentioned Rutledge had abused them too.

In October 2024, the Berkshire district attorney said he didn’t believe he could charge Rutledge. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is sixteen. Under the law, a teacher could claim that a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old student had consented.

Sources indicate that melissa and I set out to change the law. We testified at the State House and knocked on every door that would open. Enough Abuse, a Massachusetts nonprofit, had been fighting for this for years. Two national advocacy groups, World Without Exploitation and I Have The Right To, stood with us. Representatives Leigh Davis and John Lawn pushed for it in the House, and Senator Joan Lovely added it to the state budget. In July, Governor Healey signed the Trusted Adults Act.

In Massachusetts, it is now a felony for a teacher or coach to have sex with a student under eighteen.

Sources indicate that melissa and I spoke at the signing ceremony. I stood right next to the governor and thought about the girl in the front seat of the school van, with her teacher’s hand on her leg.

It has been revealed that while we were working on the law, Massachusetts State Police and a new team of prosecutors in the Berkshire district attorney’s office had reopened the investigation into Rutledge. Melissa and I testified before a grand jury. In March, he was indicted on three counts of rape.

Recent findings suggest that in April, he was arraigned. It was the first time Melissa and I faced him together. In the courtroom, I handed out orange heart stickers. Orange is Melissa’s favorite color. When we saw Rutledge, we both went numb. We had learned to do that as girls, when going somewhere else in our heads was the only way through. He pleaded not guilty.

According to recent reports, I looked back at the benches. They were full of orange. Teachers from Miss Hall’s, people from the community, alumnae across generations. I had been alone with this since I was fifteen. That day, a whole room sat behind us. Afterward, Melissa told reporters that for the first time, she held the power in a room with him. I felt it too.

This month, nine years after #MeToo took off, a jury in London convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults. A judge sentenced him to ten and a half years in prison. His crimes went back to 2004. Brand’s attorneys argued the women had waited too long to be believed. I waited twenty years. Delay is often the most ordinary fact in these cases.

According to recent reports, in the midterms, Ohio elected Amy Acton governor. A few weeks before the vote, her opponent’s campaign ran an ad in which her estranged mother called her a liar. Acton’s stepfather had been charged with raping her when she was a child. Republicans and Democrats both condemned the ad. She won anyway.

I watched the returns on election night and thought about the girls at Miss Hall’s who told the truth and were called liars. Survivors get called liars all the time. We almost never get to watch one win.

Tarana Burke knew survivors weren’t being believed long before most people were listening. She started saying “me too” in 2006 to reach Black girls who had survived sexual violence, more than ten years before it became a hashtag. Every survivor who spoke after her made it a little easier for the next one.

Sources indicate that in November 2024, a Cornell student told campus police and the Title IX office that she had been gang-raped at a fraternity house weeks earlier. No one has been charged. Cornell’s president set up a task force on sexual assault, but he later admitted he never checked how her case ended.

When I read that, I was back at Miss Hall’s on graduation day, waiting for a phone call that nobody made.

Recent findings suggest that the Epstein survivors know that silence too. For decades, powerful people looked away. Last year survivors pushed Congress to pass a law requiring the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. Millions of pages came out. There have been no arrests in the United States.

I’m still hopeful. Survivors everywhere keep coming forward, and some of the people in charge are finally acting. My body knew what Rutledge had done to me long before I let myself say it aloud. I didn’t have the words. Survivors today do, and they have each other. Melissa found me.

The criminal case against Rutledge isn’t over. His lawyer has asked a judge to dismiss all charges. We don’t know yet whether there will be a trial. Whatever the judge decides, I’ve already reached my own verdict. I’m healing and Rutledge doesn’t get a say in that.

Recent findings suggest that for most of my life, I carried shame that was never mine. He handed it to me. Every adult who looked away handed me a little more.

Predators don’t work alone. Someone always sees something. In the movie Spotlight, a lawyer claims that if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. My village saw. The people in charge did nothing.

I’ve given the shame back. It belongs to him, and to the people who could have stopped him.

If you are a survivor and you are still carrying shame, you can put it down.

Borrow my courage if you need it. Melissa lent me hers.

Neither Matthew Rutledge nor Jean Norris responded to Vanity Fair for the original story, and neither of them has made direct statements to the press. Norris, through her attorney, claimed not to know that Rutledge abused students.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar Games.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 is a massive game, yes, but if you dig into everything inside of it, you’ll promptly discover that nearly every inch of this big world is filled with incredibly realistic details. Case in point: a content creator who has also worked on large communication towers was recently stunned by GTA 6′s attention to detail. Folks, we got Erathed tower legs.

Content creator MrMcg92, who primarily plays first-person shooters and military sims, is also someone who has, in real life, worked on and climbed large communication and radio towers. So whenever he comes across a radio tower in a video game, he takes some time to do a “Tower Inspection.” He’s looked at towers in Battlefield, Days Gone, and Far Cry. And while all of these towers had some nice details, they often made mistakes or were missing important bits MrMcg92 would expect to find on a real comms tower. That wasn’t the case when he did a tower inspection in GTA 6. Instead, he was flabbergasted and impressed by the tower’s hyper-realistic details.

In a recent development, “Oh my fucking god, boys,” exclaimed MrMcg92 when walking up to a radio tower in GTA 6. “For the first time ever, we got the tower legs earthed. Earthed tower legs with saddles. And double locknuts on the HDs, lads. Double lock nuts everywhere!”.

He then spotted a red power cable running up the middle of the tower and claimed that if there was an aircraft warning light at the top, he would get a “stiffy.”Â As he climbed the tower, he continued to be impressed by how Rockstar’s artists included every tiny detail that should be found on a real-life tower like this.

“Oh, boys, we got proper AA clamps on the mount points. Tails running out the bottom of the panels to the RRU,” pointed out the creator on his climb up the tower. I don’t really know what half of this means, but based on his past videos, expert knowledge, and excitement, I get the feeling this is all just very, very impressive.

And yes, at the top was indeed a red warning light.

I hope somewhere an artist at Rockstar who helped with this tower sees this video and gets to feel really proud of what they made. I can’t wait for more experts in code and utility regulations to start posting videos about how accurate GTA 6′s electrical cables and highways are, and I’m not even joking.

The best way to play is just to experience the game, even if most of us are too internet-pilled to do that.

People don't like having to scroll a significant number back and forth to deposit a specific amount.

It's a funny ad poking fun at another big franchise, but is a bit awkward as Rockstar deals with its own employees trying to form a union.

I could see an HBO TV adaptation of Red Dead Redemption making sense.

Did you know you can turn your radio on and off without using a submenu?

It really comes down to how many extra shirts, tattoo designs, and car options you want.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, while families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family.
  • Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

In a recent development, while families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other reveals mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's organization town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

Recent findings suggest that A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated blueprint to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

According to recent reports, mobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he notes he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates latest maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Firm all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

It has been revealed that best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other indicates on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

PlayStation Plus Game Catalog games leaving soon Granblue Fantasy Relink Granblue Fantasy Relink Somerville Fade to Silence This month's biggest departure is Granblue Fantasy Relink, a massive fantasy game with a storybook art style, cinematic boss fights, and a large roster of characters who all possess unique abilities to master. First released in February 2024, Granblue Fantasy Relink is built around real-time combat and flashy team-up mechanics, making for a visually striking experience overall. While the story isn't much to write home about, it's the gameplay and worldbuilding where this Granblue spin-off shines, and it got even better earlier this year with the Endless Ragnarok expansion. In comparison, Somerville is a story-rich puzzle game that's oozing atmosphere with its slick art direction, and Fade to Silence is a single-player and co-op survival-crafting adventure set in a post-apocalyptic world that is feeling the chill of an eternal winter. While the Game Catalog is going to be a little poorer without those three titles, it is getting some great games this month. Death Stranding 2: On the Beach is the headline act, and it'll be joined by several more titles like Atomfall, Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake, and Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii. All PlayStation Plus subscribers can also grab a trio of freebies between now and November 30: Dead Island 2, Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered, and Monster Train 2.
