Minor spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Recent findings suggest that the Hunger Games movies (which are streaming with a Hulu subscription) have entertained audiences for over ten years, and we've got yet another book to screen adaptation in theaters now thanks to Francis Lawrence's Sunrise on the Reaping film. My favorite scene from the book was unfortunately cut from the prequel movie, and I had to ask both the director and actress Mckenna Grace about it.

According to recent reports, I loved the Sunrise on the Reaping book, and was wildly impressed by how well it was adapted for film. Unfortunately, the scene where Maysilee kills a Gamemaker alongside District 4 career Maritte didn't make it. As you can see in the video above, I asked Francis Lawrence about this decision, where he confirmed the sequence was shot during principal photography. In his words:.

Sources indicate that it's probably the most debated sequence that we had throughout the development process. What happens is, because of that action with the game makers and because of the fight that happens with Maysilee and Haymitch after, it was a fight that in the book is about implicit submission. And the argument that some of us had was that he was already no longer submitting. Like, you know, if you've been down to Sub A, if you've done the things that he's done without spoiler in this movie he's not submitting anymore. And so it didn't feel like it thematically fit.

Points were made. While it would have been awesome to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker, in the novel it's connected to her relationship with Haymitch. They have an argument afterward about him still implicitly submitting to The Capitol, and not killing the Gamemakers despite being the closest Tribute to them. As director Francis Lawrence told me, that confrontation between the District 12 tributes didn't make sense for the movie adaptation, especially after following Joseph Zada's protagonist as he attempted to break The Arena.

This sequence was indeed shot, so the debate about whether or not to include it in Sunrise on the Reaping extended to the post-production phase. As the director went on to tell me:.

We shot it. We even augmented the fight to be, tried to be about different things. And then that thematically didn't fit. And so we ended up cutting it from the movie, but I believe will be one of the deleted scenes that will be available.

It has been revealed that fingers crossed that we get to see this scene sometime in the future, via special features when the latest Hunger Games prequel is released to homes. This isn't the only change made to Sunrise on the Reaping, which included some references to Lucy Gray Baird from Songbirds and Snakes. Of course, I had to ask the actress who brought Maysilee to life about the cut sequence.

While interviewing the cast of the new Hunger Games movie, I asked Mckenna Grace about Maysilee's cut scene. She spoke about the argument with Joseph Zada's Haymitch that followed the Gamemaker death, telling me:.

And so it just didn't make, it didn't make sense for them to be so split at that time whenever their bond had just become so strong. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, video game consoles are more expensive than ever, but sales are growing regardless, at least in the US. Circana has released its report for US video game industry sales in October, confirming that PS5 unit sales increased by 5% compared to October 2025. That's despite the average selling price of a PS5 increasing by 13%. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY Xbox Series X|S unit sales jumped by 10% in October 2026 compared to October 2025, and the average selling price rose by 29% year-over-year. The Switch 2 was October 2026's top console in unit and dollar sales, and it remains 2026's best-performing console by those measurements, followed by PS5. However, Circana did not break out the specifics for Switch 2 unit sales or average selling price changes. Total hardware spending in the US on game consoles was up by 2%, reaching $357 million. Higher pricing drove the dollar sales growth, Circana said, noting that PS5 dollar sales rose by 20% and Xbox Series X|S jumped by 42%. However, Switch 2 sales, measured by dollar sales, fell by 11%. Looking back to September 2026, PS5 hardware dollar sales grew by 43%, while spending on Xbox Series X|S dropped by 2% and Switch 2 fell by 12%. It will be interesting to see the November US hardware data when it comes in, as experts have said the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S could get a jolt in sales from people buying systems to play GTA 6. However, Circana has warned that sales might not be as strong as expected due to the increased prices. Microsoft, Sony, and Nintendo have raised prices on their consoles due in part to the ongoing memory and component shortages from the AI buildout. Tariffs have also played a role. On the subject of tariffs, all three received refunds from the government after the Supreme Court deemed the tariffs illegal, but those companies are keeping the money and not giving anything back to you. The companies argued that people who paid more knew what they were doing and don't deserve to get any money back.

Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

It has been revealed that the Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified Newly introduced York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage).

Sources indicate that guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

It has been revealed that chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

Singer-songwriter girlsweetvoiced.

GTA 6’s Digital Release Has GameStop CEO Defending Physical Games, For Obvious Reasons

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The GTA 6 launch looks set to break several records, as the digital-only game appears on track to be a major critical and commercial hit.
  • The GTA 6 launch looks set to break several records, as the digital-only game appears on track to be a major critical and commercial hit.
  • "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it, or lend it to a friend," Cohen remarked to Bloomberg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The GTA 6 launch looks set to break several records, as the digital-only game appears on track to be a major critical and commercial hit. Right on cue, GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen has criticized publishers that forgo a traditional physical release as a business strategy that hurts consumers and GameStop's bottom line, without explicitly mentioning GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it, or lend it to a friend," Cohen said to Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all-digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop. Of course they don't like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying newly introduced. They're taking away competition." https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RQvBOySNq1U Cohen's comments come in the wake of GTA 6 being a digital-only release--the "physical" edition includes a download code for it. It's also somewhat ironic for Cohen to defend physical games, given the GameStop boss's July remarks that physical video games were "irrelevant" to GameStop's business strategy. That business model has relied heavily on secondhand game sales, and none of those profits ever made their way back to the original publishers. Presently, GameStop says that selling video game software makes up the smallest part of its business. But in the case of GTA 6? Going digital probably made financial sense for Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games. The entire game clocks in at over 211GB, which means three standard 100GB Ultra HD Blu-ray discs would have been needed to house GTA 6 in its launch-day entirety--although realistically, Take-Two probably would have opted for one disc and forced consumers to download the rest of the game. That would have raised costs, and it wouldn't be unlikely to imagine Take-Two fearing the discs being reverse-engineered for secrets ahead of GTA 6's launch. Going digital essentially removed those risks, and while PlayStation and Xbox do take a cut of profits for hosting the game on their servers. According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 sales for PS5 alone have reached $1.38 billion in revenue so far, which means Sony is profiting handsomely from those sales. Retailers are still entitled to a share of the profits for stocking the code-in-a-box version of the game on their shelves, and once you start to factor in distribution costs, Take-Two's reasoning starts to make sense. The publisher says 98% of its business is digital, but it's not ruling out a proper physical GTA 6 edition in the future. Why GTA 6 Doesn’t Include Disney World

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida.
  • Walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida.
  • It has been revealed that rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson said the decision to came down to resources and story reasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that walt Disney World is synonymous with Florida, but the iconic theme park doesn't show up in Rockstar's GTA 6, which takes place in a fictional Florida called Leonida. Many are wondering why, especially when GTA: Vice City had its own parody of the theme park--Fun World--many years ago. Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson remarked the decision to came down to resources and story reasons. “A theme park would represent a lot of work that we didn’t have, and we didn’t have a strong narrative reason to send them there,” he told VGC. Nelson added that Rockstar isn't known to cut corners, so if GTA 6 were to have its own version of Walt Disney World, it would be a "fully functioning theme park," and that just wasn't doable. Walt Disney World is much more than just its most famous park, Magic Kingdom. The property includes three other main parks, Animal Kingdom, Hollywood Studios, and Epcot, along with the Disney Springs shopping district, multiple water parks and golf courses, and more than two-dozen hotels. The entire property is more than 25,000 acres. Even if Rockstar were to replicate only a portion of the scale of the real Walt Disney World, it would surely be a big job. Players might expect fully functioning rides, and Nelson said the challenge for Rockstar would be, "Where do you stop? When do you feel like it's enough?" Nelson said people think Rockstar has unlimited time and money, and that isn't true. "So sometimes you just have to admit we are not going to be able to make this to the level we feel we need to,” he said. Plus, as Nelson pointed out, there would need to be a story reason to send Jason and Lucia hundreds of miles north from Miami to Orlando, where Walt Disney World is. GTA 6 has a huge map, but it's contained to Vice City and its surrounding areas--it doesn't go that far north.

Robert Pattinson Is the Newly introduced James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.
  • That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes.
  • Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

According to recent reports, A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

Daniel Craig, Casino Royale, 2006.

Industry observers note that as portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

Sources indicate that when Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Roger Moore, The Spy Who Loved Me, 1977.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Recent findings suggest that also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first newly introduced Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Industry observers note that of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the organization acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

In a recent development, pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

It has been revealed that in September, Pattinson was declared as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this upcoming installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the massive screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

In a recent development, the real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave fresh world of brand deals, anything is possible.

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was a free patch to the beloved roguelike that arrived on PC in 2024, but launched on console earlier this week in a head-to-head matchup against Grand Theft Auto 6. The marketing stunt may have been a success, but AI-generated music tracks discovered in a special fresh Vice City mode have turned the launch into a nightmare.

Industry observers note that while Repentance+ came to PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2 this week, the Steam version of the game also got a free upgrade. “Be sure to get in and play today’s Daily Run for a very special crime-packed surprise. Enter the Basement, and go out in a glorious blaze of bullets and vehicular homicide!” read the patch notes on on Valve’s storefront. Players could enter the seed “V1CE BSMT” into the roguelike before starting their run to launch a GTA-inspired version with special weapons and music.

Earlier today, however, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted a comprehensive breakdown of the new music tracks alleging they were made with Suno, an AI-based music generation tool. “The new revision includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),” the wrote. The post continued:.

In a recent development, some include Suno metadata with them. You can find this information yourself by just checking the file comment metadata (something common like VLC has tools for this, but here’s ffprobe output of drivingsong1.ogg, for example):.

comment : made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z; id=cd5a5b55-bead-4cb9-949d-09ed1f917dce.

Other files have this comment scrubbed; they were edited/exported later, but nonetheless there’s the proof.

Recent findings suggest that please report concerns and bugs to the email attached. https://t.co/KHKSqKGsUe.

— ð Edmund McMillen ð (@edmundmcmillen) November 21, 2026.

Sources indicate that “They’ve had how long now to prepare the GTA 6 release Easter egg daily run literally nobody asked for and still ai slopped it? Are you fucking kidding me,” one fan wrote on the Binding of Isaac subreddit. “No shit, itâs 2026. The entire industry is like this. Cutting corners constantly because they know they can get away with it,” wrote another.

It has been revealed that many have blamed Nicalis, the publisher and co-developer of the Repentance+ expansion, in particular. Complaints about ongoing bugs, latency, and quality control issues have seemingly been building for some time. The latest mishap results in a review-bomb of the expansion’s Steam page, which currently sits at an abysmal user rating of just 9 percent positive. “AI generated music in GTA mode; Edmund please take back control of the game,” reads one of the latest Steam reviews. “Not to mention there’s like single digit bug fixes in a year+ long awaited enhancement with no other changes.”.

The AI music was news to Edmund McMillen, the game’s creator. “Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned,” he posted earlier today on X. An emergency update has since gone out to remove the AI-generated music as well as address some other versions with the latest version of the expansion, but Nicalis has yet to take responsibility for the use of AI or explained how it made it into the game.

Steam requires store page disclosures for any content that uses assets generated with the help of AI, which The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+Â did not have, despite the substantial publicity push around the latest revision and it landing on the same day as Rockstar’s open-world blockbuster. “That was [Nicalis’] idea,” McMillen recently told Eurogamer. “‘Wouldn’t it be funny if…?’ I was like, whatever, that’s funny…We’re done, so we’ve got to release this month…It’s a fun experiment.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as of late, it feels like all our favorite former Disney Channel stars are tying the knot! Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco said “I do” last September, Zendaya is officially married and this weekend, it’s Miley Cyrus’ turn! Now, we have a glimpse of what her rehearsal dinner looked like, and the details are gorgeous.

Sources indicate that miley Cyrus is getting married to fellow musician Maxx Morando. The couple have been together since they met on a blind date back in 2021. The pair recently had a classy rehearsal dinner attended by their loved ones, including Cyrus’ stepsister Lily Purcell. Amid the event, Purcell shared some snapshots, and you can check out one below:.

This looks so romantic! Guests were treated to a three-course meal including filet mignon, Maine lobster ravioli and a trio of desserts. I especially love the “M+M” touch on the top of the menu for the affair. Purcell, who’s the daughter of Tish Cyrus’ husband, actor Dominic Purcell, also showcased the end-of-meal treats on her Instagram story with this photo:.

It has been revealed that if you’re curious, that’s a chocolate caramel layer cake, vanilla crème brûlée and raspberry sorbet for dessert. Yum! It also looks like Purcell was also sipping on an espresso martini. The rehearsal dinner was reportedly in an undisclosed location in Los Angeles on Friday night ahead of Cyrus and Morando reportedly getting married this weekend.

Sources indicate that per reports, the rehearsal dinner was a very intimate affair, with just around 20 people in attendance. This weekend has been a long time coming, as Morando proposed to Cyrus while they were on a trip to Kyoto, Japan in 2025. At that time, Morando -- who had been with Cyrus for four years by that point -- surprised her by getting down on one knee while in a garden.

Sources indicate that this is Cyrus’ second wedding, as she previously tied the knot with Liam Hemsworth back in 2018 in Nashville, Tennessee. Ultimately, the Last Song stars separated less than a year after the wedding and finalized their divorce in 2020.

Career-wise, Cyrus released her tenth studio album, Bass Persuades, back in September. The album includes the very apt track “Let’s Get Married,” with the music video even featuring Cyrus and Morando together. Morando also joined Cyrus on stage to play drums during the song during her first significant concert in years at the Hollywood Bowl last month.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Other than that, Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando have remained pretty private over the years. We first heard of their engagement when Cyrus turned up to an event for Avatar: Fire and Ash last year with Morando and had a ring on her finger. Time will tell if Cyrus and Morando will showcase their actual wedding or keep it under wraps, but I’d imagine the latter. Either way, I'm so happy for the couple, and love seeing the gorgeous rehearsal dinner spread in celebration of their love.

#85834. Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall.
  • It has been revealed that this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes.
  • In a recent development, both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall. For now, I’ll accept that it is Cruz because the image is on a poster for Broken Embraces, a 2009 film she starred in. My hesitation in believing it’s her, however, is because finding a resemblance between the woman on the poster and Cruz requires a lot of generosity. It’s as if the artist had painted her based on a detailed description he’d heard, but he’d never actually seen his subject onscreen. “We were given this in India,” explains Pedro Almodóvar’s brother, Agustín, the head and owner of El Deseo, the production company behind Almodóvar’s films. “Specialized artists still hand-paint their movie posters, and the results are images like this.” The work’s imperfections give it a charm that no poster created by AI could ever match.

It has been revealed that this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. It depicts a Blade Runner–style dystopian future where replicants, jaded by digital perfection, are fascinated by the rough edges of human culture. The book has just been published in Spain (it is scheduled to be published in the United States, in Spanish, in February 2027), following the release of Almodóvar’s latest film, Bitter Christmas (which will be in select US theaters on November 13, and released nationwide on November 25).

In a recent development, both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator. At the same time, they are clearly different from Almodóvar, like the difference between Cruz and the woman on the Indian movie poster.

I ask Almodóvar why he decided to recount Flavio’s story in the form of a novel rather than a movie, but he appears to have not heard my question and answers instead as if I’d asked him why it took him so long to publish a novel, which is undoubtedly much more interesting: “I think the reason I hadn’t written a novel until now was that I wasn’t sure I’d be able to, even though I’d wanted to write one since I was a young man. At first, however, I didn’t even know myself that this story would be a novel. I started with a simple anecdote about an acting coach and an actor, and that opened the floodgates; the story began to pour out. When it was already over 30 pages, I sent it to my editor. He told me there was a novel there and that I should keep going.”.

The 77-year-old director from La Mancha poses in a jacket, polo shirt, pants, and sneakers by Loewe.

It has been revealed that he will answer many other questions that I haven’t asked but should have: “I didn’t know, for example, that I’d include my story ‘Addiction,’ which is a little treat for fans that had already appeared in Pain and Glory. It was going to be a monologue that Carmen Machi would perform in a small theater, but I ended up giving it to Asier Etxeandia in that film. I also wrote Pain and Glory very swiftly. And in it, I inserted, like little snippets, more pieces that I’d already written. For example, there’s another story, just five pages long, about a chance encounter with an actor with whom I’d had a very bad relationship in the past [Eusebio Poncela, who starred in Law of Desire 40 years ago] and with whom, in the story, I ended up doing heroin. In real life, the fact that he was using heroin while we were filming was the reason we had a falling out. Thanks to those preexisting elements, which fit into the story, I was able to write that movie so quickly. And the same is true of my new book. What defines it is a sense of absolute freedom.”.

And maybe that sentence is, in the end, the answer to all my questions for Almodóvar.

Vanity Fair España: Is that sense of freedom why you decided to write a novel instead of a screenplay?

Sources indicate that pedro Almodóvar: In Bitter Christmas, Leonardo Sbaraglia’s character states he needs absolute freedom to work. Just like me throughout my entire career. That freedom feels more intense with a novel because it’s a format with which I have less experience. I’ve woven it together from different stories, but they all revolve around the protagonist and it’s been very satisfying. It wasn’t a whim: The book has the same rigor to it as everything else I do, but that freedom is deeply rooted in my style. That’s why I wrote it so quickly. Everything flowed naturally.

In a recent development, there is a tradition of using a novel as a container for many stories, as with Don Quixote or Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. On the other hand, speaking of influences, it’s interesting that when you wrote your Patty Diphusa stories in 1983 [included in Patty Diphusa and Other Writings, published by Faber & Faber in 1992], Anita Loos and pornographic photo novels are influences that appear in the mix, but in The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes, you turn to, let’s say, more distinguished names: Henry James, Nabokov, and Colm Tóibín, who even appears as a character.

I’m not trying to compare myself to Cervantes or Potocki, but yes, that’s what the book is. That’s precisely why this novel can’t be adapted for the screen: You’d have to choose one part of it and develop it, but as it stands now, that wouldn’t be possible. Those earlier influences are still with me—Anita Loos is certainly among them—and they continue to inspire me with both specific phrases and broader themes. In the novel, I name authors who inspire me and with whom I connect organically, such as Joan Didion and Virginia Woolf. But Patty and Flavio have something in common: a sense of urgency that drives them to write at a breakneck pace, out of a physiological need. Neither of them sleeps much, though in Patty’s case it’s because she can’t stop doing cocaine. Beyond that, other differences set them apart, including the differences between what life was like in the ’80s and what it’s like now.

What sort of differences are there, and where are they most apparent?

It has been revealed that take sex, for example. Patty Diphusa is an archetype of the 1980s, a time of absolute freedom in Spain, and her character can only be understood in the context of the utterly carefree and hedonistic lifestyle we led back then. If she sucks a guy's dick in a bathroom, she’ll then record her wild thoughts because she considers herself a sort of philosopher of eroticism. Although Flavio is a very free-spirited person, just like the book itself, he belongs to another era and another generation. Here, sex is part of a love story, and his attitude toward it is very different. I devote less space to the erotic scenes in this book because I assume people already know what it’s like to sleep with someone.

Almodóvar, in another room at El Deseo’s headquarters, wearing a Louis Vuitton jacket and a Prada knit polo shirt.

You’ve argued on different occasions that in the 1980s, many people in Spain chose that hedonistic and seemingly frivolous lifestyle as a reaction to the previous era, and that this was a political statement. Now we see a new generation adopting a different kind of stance. For example, all across Europe, people are taking to the streets to demand their right to housing and decent living conditions, and there’s not much frivolity in that. How do you interpret this change?

In a recent development, I completely empathize with and support the people filling the streets. They are demanding fundamental rights that are enshrined in the Spanish constitution and which are now in jeopardy: housing, health care, and education. I went to the encampment on the Puerta del Sol [in Madrid] only a few times, because I was in New York presenting Bitter Christmas at the New York Film Festival and also because I think a famous person doesn’t really fit in at these demonstrations—if we go, we distort the spirit of it. But I did go, and I bought them food because that’s what I thought they’d need, even though they told me they’d be better off with some tables. I don’t just support their initiative; I’m glad it happened. One thing I’d heard about young people, a generation I don’t know much about, was from a news article that said that 25% of young Spaniards wouldn’t mind living under a dictatorship like Franco’s. I shuddered. What happened in the Puerta del Sol shows that there’s a whole crowd of young people beyond those who go to Ferraz to pray the rosary [since November 2023, a group of Catholic protesters has gathered daily to pray outside the headquarters of the PSOE, Spain’s socialist party, on Madrid’s Calle Ferraz]. They aren’t rich, and they don’t have their lives figured out; they can’t work in the professions they studied to pursue, and they don’t earn enough money to buy homes. That’s terrifying. And the political parties have shown their true colors when it comes to housing. Of course, the PSOE is late to the game with the so-called Maricarmen decrees [a series of measures named after Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her home and subsequent death in October galvanized activists], but at least it has reacted. The starkly different reactions from the Partido Popular [Popular Party] and Vox [center-right and far-right parties, respectively] already tell you what they think about this issue.

Would you agree today with that line from Gloria Muñoz in The Flower of My Secret: “With so much reality, the country’s ready to explode”?

Recent findings suggest that she was talking in literary terms, but it’s true that this phrase has taken on a life of its own over time and has spilled over into other areas. The same thing has happened to another phrase: “A woman is more authentic the more she resembles the person she has dreamed of becoming,” as Agrado mentioned in All About My Mother. It was a line written for a transgender woman, and one that makes perfect sense for her. But now it can be understood in relation to any kind of character: It speaks to authenticity, to staying true to oneself and to one’s own dreams. In the case of young people in our country, we’re talking about a social reality. The country has changed a lot, and we’re very polarized—though France is even worse off than Spain. Europe is in very bad shape overall. The kind of news coverage being produced plays a major role in this rise of the far right. Since the images promoted by the right are so jarring and sensationalist, TV stations pick up on them, and in doing so, they’re effectively promoting figures like Vito Quiles [a far-right activist and influencer]. Damn it, don’t put Vito Quiles on TV—it’s better if we don’t even know where he is or what he’s doing!

Are you particularly concerned about the attention that the far right is getting?

People like [Santiago] Abascal [president of the Vox political party] and [Javier]Milei [president of Argentina] want to do away with the state. Milei, the biggest loudmouth of them all, even aims to destroy the state from within the state itself, which is diabolical. I cite Milei as an example because he claims so himself. And on top of that, people elect him for that very reason: He’s someone who has come to power democratically, just like [Donald] Trump. So we’re putting the tools of democracy in the hands of someone whose main goal is to destroy it. Furthermore, in a world so polarized—and with a far right that has no qualms about calling itself fascist—the emergence of AI creates a perfect storm.

One of the stories in your book is, in fact, a dystopian tale inspired by Blade Runner, in which large corporations with shadowy agendas seek to create a less human world. You have contributed so much to human creativity. Are you concerned about how that creativity is being taken over by AI?

I’m always open to change. It’s necessary for society to move forward. But I think the encroachment of AI on human agency is terrible. They should start regulating it now. I’m concerned about the jobs it will replace and also the synthetic culture it will create. In fact, a synthetic culture based on data already exists, and it lacks a soul. The genesis of a screenplay must be human, because AI doesn’t have the sense of doubt, the patience, or the capacity for stories to build up layers of meaning, as in Talk to Her and Bad Education. We need a society that cares about culture, promotes it, and supports it, and not a soulless culture focused only on the immediate. I haven’t used AI creatively, nor do I really know how to. But I’m concerned that we’re now unable to tell whether an image is real or not, given the level of perfection this technology has reached. And moreover, behind it all are very powerful people who know no limits.

Industry observers note that on another topic, standards of beauty have changed, with cosmetic surgery and fillers now widely prevalent. For someone who places such importance on the expressions of actors that must also be a cause for concern.

According to recent reports, well, I wouldn’t mind if an actor in one of my movies had had plastic surgery. For example, I wouldn’t turn down Nicole Kidman for that reason—she’s not only a great actor, but she has also had plastic surgery, and she looks better than ever. Because, these days, actors who’ve had plastic surgery are part of the landscape. It’s so common that you no longer have to explain that a character has had it done; it’s accepted as a matter of course. What’s more, cosmetic surgery has advanced so much that high-profile figures who’ve had work done—like Donatella Versace, Lindsay Lohan, or Nicole Kidman herself—have completely erased the signs of their previous procedures with splendid results. [Editor’s note: Lindsay Lohan has denied having a facelift, while Kidman has never confirmed undergoing any plastic surgery.] The big problem is that, if you make films set in the past, you can’t cast women with plastic surgery or lip fillers; it would be anachronistic, just like putting a piece of furniture from the 1980s in a film about the Spanish Civil War. But it’s true that in my films, plastic surgery hasn’t usually been an option, for aesthetic reasons. Fortunately, there will always be people like Frances McDormand and Carmen Maura. We need older women who look their age.

In a recent development, what interests me most about your fresh novel is the protagonist’s relationship with an actor, Alez Mazado—a sex symbol who isn’t very intelligent but has a certain natural talent and is open to being molded. Flavio is his Pygmalion. There’s even an explicit reference to Hitchcock’s film Vertigo, which also features that kind of relationship. Do you often have that kind of dynamic with your actors?

Recent findings suggest that I’m like Jimmy Stewart in Vertigo: With actors, I get involved in their hair, lip color, outfits—everything. When I watched Vertigo for the umpteenth time, I thought that character was a director: “He knows exactly what he wants,” they tell him when he takes Kim Novak to try on outfits at a store. The actors I work with and I have adapted to each other, just like in a marriage—in my films, they speak differently; the actors themselves say so. Aitana Sánchez-Gijón told me that she felt she could do anything after playing her role in Bitter Christmas. But I work differently with each actor. With Penélope, for example, I rehearse a lot, and the more we rehearse, the better she gets; then I shoot many takes, and the 10th one is better than the third. And if I can shoot 12, even better. But others don’t like to rehearse, like Antonio Banderas, because he’s a different kind of actor. He has extraordinary intuition and instinct. I don’t need to talk to him as much or push him so hard.

People talk about Los Javis [the moniker for actors turned directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo] as your natural heirs, in the wake of the success of La Bola Negra, which you coproduced through El Deseo. Do you think they will continue your creative legacy?

They definitely treat me like their mentor. They know entire films of mine by heart, even lines that I don’t remember. They’ve been deeply influenced by my films, just as I’ve been influenced by [Luis García] Berlanga, [Rafael] Azcona, [Luis] Buñuel, and [Carlos] Saura. Even if you don’t want to admit it, everyone has role models. I find it flattering, but to say they’re my heirs is to minimize their work. They have a style all their own. In fact, if I were to write the screenplay for La Bola Negra, it would be very different. I don’t feel like their father. I take responsibility for my films and nothing else.

How do you view their film’s unstoppable run at the awards and at the box office?

Los Javis are the big thing right now. Their film is going to be the highest-grossing Spanish movie of all time, although I don’t remember how much The Last Torch Song (1957), starring Sara Montiel, made back in the day. At El Deseo, we’ve had two fantastic years—first with Oliver Laxe’s film [Sirāt], which we also coproduced, and now this one. And I hope the Javis can keep on going and make it through the rest of their promotional tour and then the awards season. From my experience as an Oscar nominee, I know the best moment isn’t when they call your name, but when the ceremony ends. That’s when your life is your own again—whether to start on the next project or simply sleep if that’s what you prefer.

Have you shared that experience with the Javis? Do you give them advice?

Industry observers note that just yesterday I texted Javier Ambrossi, and he told me they’ve already had enough. And they have no idea what’s still in store for them! We’ll meet next week, and I’ll explain it all to him. At the Oscars, they’re the favorites in the best-international-feature-film category; they’re a sure thing. Although I experienced that curse of being the front-runner when Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown was the favorite and then Pelle the Conqueror ended up winning—a film no one even remembers now. But anyway, everyone now expects La Bola Negra to be nominated in other categories as well, which is historic for our film industry. It’s great for us.

On a recent podcast, one of the actors from La Bola Negra, Yenesi, described the film as Federico García Lorca fan fiction—which is actually quite fitting, since its entire narrative is built on elements related to Lorca’s life and writings. Roland Barthes had already spoken of the death of the author, and Eugenio d’Ors famously stated, “There is no true originality outside tradition. Everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.”.

According to recent reports, I’ve written that phrase down! I read it in one of [journalist and writer Francisco] Umbral’s columns; I suppose he got it from d’Ors.

In other words, Umbral appropriated it for himself, and in doing so, he proved its enduring relevance.

It’s inevitable that the things you like will influence your work. And the things you hate too. When you write, you have a general idea of the story, but as you develop it, what you create is rooted in things that are part of your life. And your life always resembles the things you’ve seen before. I’m fascinated by the phenomenon of fan fiction because of its contradictory nature; it’s a miracle that an entire culture has developed around this phenomenon, which exists outside the mainstream market yet at the same time feeds off the most mainstream works, such as Star Trek or Star Wars. Fan fiction is a declaration of love for the original and proof that great stories never end: There will always be someone to continue them. Just as people don’t die as long as there’s someone who remembers them.

Of course I have to ask you, with the promotional tour for Bitter Christmas coming to an end, what are you working on next?

Well, it was going to be a comedy, but after I finished it, even though I was 90% passionate about it, I realized there was something about the supporting characters that I didn’t like. So I’ve put it on hold, as I’ve done before with other projects. And now I’m writing something else. I’m well into it, but I can’t say anything. They’ll kill me if I do. It’ll be based on a book, and we’re at the moment working out the rights. This one will have plenty of humor too. Because I know for sure that, after Bitter Christmas, I don’t want to talk about myself anymore. I need different characters. And humor too.

Is there any movie you wish you’d made but that’s missing from your filmography?

There are several recent films I would have loved to have made. For example, Drive My Car by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet. Or Sentimental Value by Joachim Trier. I mean, I should have made that movie! It has everything: the cinema, a house, a father and his daughters. Everything.

Should we just accept, by the way, that you won’t make your own movie about the Spanish Civil War? Or was Parallel Mothers already your take on it?

When I read Cosamala, Alana S. Portero’s latest book, I really wanted to adapt it. But it’s such a wonderful work of literature that translating it into images would greatly diminish the wonder and surprise of her writing. If the book proves anything, it’s that Alana is a tremendous writer. I’d have to find another angle from which to tell the story of the civil war. But I do want to do it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russell Brand reportedly struggled to remember when he was married to Katy Perry during a deposition last year.
  • Brand, 51, was questioned by New York authorities in 2025 after an extra from his 2011 movie Arthur sued the disgraced comedian for alleged sexual assault, according to court documents obtained by the Daily Mail on Friday, November 20.
  • Sources indicate that in a transcript from Brand’s testimony, he seemingly failed to accurately recall the correct timeline when asked whether he was married at the time of the alleged incident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russell Brand reportedly struggled to remember when he was married to Katy Perry during a deposition last year.

Brand, 51, was questioned by New York authorities in 2025 after an extra from his 2011 movie Arthur sued the disgraced comedian for alleged sexual assault, according to court documents obtained by the Daily Mail on Friday, November 20.

Sources indicate that in a transcript from Brand’s testimony, he seemingly failed to accurately recall the correct timeline when asked whether he was married at the time of the alleged incident. (The anonymous victim claimed that Brand exposed himself to her and sexually assaulted her in a bathroom on set.).

Recent findings suggest that “Whilst I — of course, it wouldn’t be difficult for me to find out whether or not I was married, because it would be on the internet somewhere, I’m assuming,” Brand said, per court documents. “I was — what I do know is that I was in a relationship with, as you know, obviously a very high-profile woman. And even when I was married to her, I was sort of drowning in love.”.

Industry observers note that perry, 42, and Brand started dating in 2009, one year before they got married. The now-exes divorced in 2011. (Us has reached out to reps for both Perry and Brand for comment regarding the alleged deposition comments.).

In a recent development, perry, who shares 6-year-old daughter Daisy with ex Orlando Bloom, has since moved on with former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau. Brand, for his part, has been married to Laura Gallacher since 2017.

Recent findings suggest that gallacher, who shares three kids with Brand, has remained by his side in the wake of his sexual misconduct trial and subsequent conviction. Brand was first accused of assault in 2023, vehemently denying the accusations and pleading not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and found not guilty on the remaining charges earlier this month and sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison.

“We trust God, and we trust his plan, and we trust everything He’s doing right now, even though it’s painful,” Gallacher noted on the Sunday, November 15, episode of the couple’s Sunday Service YouTube channel, breaking her silence on Brand’s conviction. “Obviously, [it] will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me.”.

Check our latest news in Google News.

Check our latest news in Apple News.

Gallacher also vowed to continue their joint YouTube channel in Brand’s absence.

“Although Russell is not here now in this moment, the holy spirit is moving and the holy spirit cannot be restrained,” she mentioned. “I’m speaking to Russell. He’s OK and he’s praying, unsurprisingly. He’s praying and we decided for me to continue.”.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, contact the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-HOPE (4673).

According to recent reports, the Epic Games Store continues to give away a free game each week, and this week's offering is another nice find at a price that can't be beat. Every Thursday at 8 AM PT / 11 AM ET, Epic offers at least one free PC game (and sometimes even as many as two or three). All you need to do to claim the free games is create a free Epic account and enable two-factor authentication. You have a week to add the freebies to your library before the new one(s) take their place. At this point, Epic has given away hundreds of free games, and there's no sign that the program will stop any time soon. The firm has also extended its freebies to Android devices, and you can claim a free game every week here as well. We keep this article up to date weekly to highlight both the current free games and next week's offerings. If you're looking for more freebies, you can check out our list of the 25 best free PC games to play right now, or for more options, the 25 best free games to play on multiple platforms. Next free games at Epic Next week, you can get a welcome gift pack for Firestone: Idle Clicker Online RPG, and you can help a pair of penguins out in the co-op platformer Bread & Fred. See all free games at Epic Epic Games Store free games list We're keeping a running list of every free game that Epic users have been able to claim in the past. The Epic Games Store continues to give away a free game each week, and this week's offering is another nice find at a price that can't be beat. Every Thursday at 8 AM PT / 11 AM ET, Epic offers at least one free PC game (and sometimes even as many as two or three). All you need to do to claim the free games is create a free Epic account and enable two-factor authentication. You have a week to add the freebies to your library before the upcoming one(s) take their place. At this point, Epic has given away hundreds of free games, and there's no sign that the program will stop any time soon. The manufacturer has also extended its freebies to Android devices, and you can claim a free game every week here as well. We keep this article up to date weekly to highlight both the current free games and next week's offerings.

If you're looking for more freebies, you can check out our list of the 25 best free PC games to play right now, or for more options, the 25 best free games to play on multiple platforms.

This week's free game is Mark of the Deep, a 2025 pirate-themed adventure with a mix of Metroidvania and soulslike gameplay.

Next week, you can get a welcome gift pack for Firestone: Idle Clicker Online RPG, and you can help a pair of penguins out in the co-op platformer Bread & Fred.

We're keeping a running list of every free game that Epic owners have been able to claim in the past. From AAA hits to indie darlings, Epic has really made its mark with free games. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it's Grand Theft Auto VI day around the world--the game is really good, as it turns out. While players are out exploring the massive in-game map or checking their in-game phones as much as they check their real-life ones, Rockstar has celebrated the occasion by releasing the full cast list for its latest crime epic. Nestled among celebrity names like Bad Bunny, "Weird Al" Yankovic, Brigitte Nielsen, Stephen Root, and Bobby Moynihan is a name that will surprise many longtime Rockstar fans. It's also, potentially, a GTA VI spoiler, so we're going to put it below a selfie of co-protagonist Jason Duval. Seriously, if you want to go into Grand Theft Auto VI spoiler-free, look away now. Do you think Jason's last name is a Jacksonville Jaguars reference? DUUUUUVAL! Alright, if you're still here, then you're in for the spoiler. Ready? Here goes: One of the names listed on the credits is Michael Hollick, playing a role known only as "The Hitman." If that's setting off a signal to established Grand Theft Auto fans, it's because Michael Hollick is also the voice of GTA IV protagonist--and occasional hitman--Niko Bellic. Hollick's involvement in GTA VI is surprising, considering how just after GTA IV's release in 2008, he publicly criticized Rockstar for his payment on the project. As reported by CNET by way of the New York Times, Hollick reportedly was paid $100,000 for 15 months of work on the project. Whether or not this is actually a spoiler remains to be seen, but with Grand Theft Auto VI now available on both PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, we imagine the truth will be revealed soon enough.

#85830. Industry News: Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield Get Real About 'Artificial'

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2436 w)
📖 Baca

Industry News: Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield Get Real About 'Artificial'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers.
  • Sources indicate that in an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s latest film, Artificial, near Altman’s house.
  • According to recent reports, “All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers. Like this one: Have Andrew Garfield and Sam Altman ever met?

Sources indicate that in an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s latest film, Artificial, near Altman’s house. Garfield—who plays Altman in the movie—remembers things differently.

According to recent reports, “All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting. I was really looking out for him,” Garfield tells me in October, shortly after Artificial’s premiere at the Fresh York Film Festival. “And I was looking at every single tinted car window. I was looking in the windows of the house. I was checking to see the security guard. No, I didn’t see him. I wish I had.”.

It’s a question that reverberates both through and around Artificial. From the start, the film has been an intriguing mash-up: a marriage between cinema’s great sensualist and the nerd kingdom of Silicon Valley. Artificial tells the story of the OpenAI CEO’s rise and fall and rise; it was cast and shot in record time to keep pace with the drumbeat of AI doomsday headlines. Then the movie became the headlines after Amazon MGM abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate—a few months after the studio’s parent organization, Amazon, invested $50 billion in OpenAI.

It has been revealed that A24 declined to rescue Artificial. So did Netflix, Focus Features, and Clockwork, the new specialty arm of Warner Bros. Finally, the lightning bolt of a feature got picked up by Neon, the distributor that’s won six consecutive Palmes d’Or at Cannes.

The film’s electric relationship to the very recent past makes it the most zeitgeist-nailing tech blockbuster since The Social Network. The difference is that back in 2010, Facebook was where you made friends on the internet. Artificial, by contrast, is a film about a self-teaching, self-aware robot that’s getting smarter by the minute and might destroy the human world. And it’s happening in real time.

Recent findings suggest that “You see, we were very prescient with things,” Guadagnino tells me. “I know my subject. I studied my subject very, very much.”.

HERE TO MAKE FRIENDS Artificial ends with a heartbreaking act of betrayal—but Guadagnino, Borisov, and Garfield left the project with their bond intact.

Artificial also has a button-pushing relationship with the truth as it endeavors to tell the real story of how OpenAI was born and investigate how reliable the people behind OpenAI are. If Altman can’t be trusted with small details—about, say, whether he ever aimed a friendly wave at Garfield—can he be trusted with the most important technology of our time?

It has been revealed that “I question the validity of his statement about being there while we were filming,” Monica Barbaro, who plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in the film, tells me. “I mean, we don’t know if that’s true. And that feels textbook to me.”.

Industry observers note that in 2024, Amazon bought a script by Simon Rich about Sam Altman and the formation of OpenAI—one of many ChatGPT-related projects then getting passed around town. Rich’s take had the backing of hit-churning producer David Heyman—the man behind Paddington and the Harry Potter series—and his script pulled no punches. To write it, Rich mined details from a childhood friend who had a job at OpenAI (and, as of now, still works there). By the end of the process, Rich was terrified of the power his friend’s colleagues commanded.

Industry observers note that “I came up with this last-ditch effort to warn mankind,” Rich said. He’s a comedy writer, but here he isn’t joking. “And I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”.

Sources indicate that after shopping the film around to directors, the studio landed on Guadagnino. To some, the Call Me by Your Name director seemed like a strange choice for a film about scientists, coders, and start-up bros. The director barely uses AI himself, or even thinks about it.

ARTIFICIAL RECKONING Garfield’s first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network.

“I think we should not let ourselves give AI such an notable role. I think for me, AI is a prop, a gadget,” Guadagnino tells me. “Definitely AI has high-end worth [for], I don’t know, the military, medicine. But in general, as a sort of everyday life usage of AI, I think it’s just a little gadget. And I don’t believe that we should ever consider the possibility that it can equal whatever we can do as people.”.

Garfield approached the material from a different vantage. By the time he got his hands on the script, the actor had been deeply invested in the Silicon Valley origin-story mythos for years—ever since he starred in that other major movie about a world-changing digital platform. His first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network. “And I thought, Oh my God,” says the actor, sitting in a suite at the Carlyle Hotel. But the movie also had its own gloss. “Simon’s script was so funny—like a stone being skimmed a thousand times across, and then a couple of really deep dives in the midst.”.

Industry observers note that making Artificial would allow Garfield to scratch an old itch. “In The Social Network, I was auditioning for [Mark] Zuckerberg. Then they found Jesse [Eisenberg],” who was much better for the role, Garfield indicates. “But it left this little dangling thread, because I started to imagine how I would play Zuckerberg: how I would try and enter that ambition and that drive and that responsibility. A kind of ability to make huge global decisions that are going to have potentially really positive effects on humanity, but inevitably, really, really heavily negative effects on humanity.”.

THE ENGINEER “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews,” indicates Borisov.

Sources indicate that garfield is not actually the lead in Artificial. The movie is focused less on Altman than on slightly naive genius coder Ilya Sutskever, played heroically by Oscar nominee Yura Borisov. Borisov has definitively never met the man he’s depicting in the film. But from afar, he can relate to Sutskever. Neither of them is quite comfortable in the spotlight.

Sources indicate that “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews because I’m every time very...I know what to say because I feel a lot about this,” the Russian actor says from a couch at the Carlyle next to Garfield. “I can see the same in his public speeches, because I’m really nervous during some public stuff.”.

Recent findings suggest that though there’s a translator next to him, Borisov soldiers through the interview with just one request for a lifeline. He adds that by cosmic coincidence, he and Sutskever have the same birthday.

Industry observers note that guadagnino was fully aware of the breakneck clip of the developing OpenAI saga. He cast his leads in days and began shooting the film in late July 2025. Artificial wrapped just two months later. As he spent the winter hunkered down in the editing room, word about the film got out. While Rich’s original script was hardly a puff piece, rumor had it that the final film leaned even harder into a negative portrayal of Altman.

Industry observers note that there’s no proof that a Jeff Bezos deal had any direct effect on decisions made by Bezos’s movie studio. But for whatever reason, late last spring, Guadagnino learned Amazon would be cutting the film loose.

All of a sudden, the speedily assembled project was in a holding pattern. The trades speculated that Amazon was deliberately killing the film to protect Altman; others wondered if the movie was being dropped not due to a conflict of interest but because it hadn’t played well in early screenings.

Barbaro pushes back on that notion. “I did believe in Luca and the film, and I had already heard really positive things from people who had seen it—really interesting positive reviews,” she states. “There is a thing these companies can do—any production company—which is to essentially build the release and squash a film. And Amazon is not a company that I think necessarily needs to make its money back on an investment like this.”.

Industry observers note that either way, it was unclear if Artificial would ever see the light of day. “It’s a dialogue between our fields: tech and art,” Borisov claims. “And I don’t know what sells, what will happen. It’s unpredictable.”.

In the end, the film was picked up by Neon—an outcome Garfield finds surprising for a few reasons. “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film, and very impressed again when they decided [that while] they didn’t want to release it, they didn’t kill it,” he claims. He pauses for a second. “They could have killed it.”.

Industry observers note that garfield’s thrilled about the film’s eventual home too. Neon, he states pointedly, is “a place for artists to be free artists.” Guadagnino feels similarly, though he claims to have zero ill will toward the studio that threw his movie to the wolves.

“I had went through a process with Amazon that I loved. They were fantastic in making this movie with me. I owe them a lot,” says Guadagnino, who’d done four films with the studio prior to Artificial: Bones and All, Challengers, Suspiria, and After the Hunt.

In a recent development, but what was it like to watch his film fall into limbo while the trades salivated over its demise? Here too, Guadagnino is blissfully zen: “Once the thing happened, I deferred to the thing. Meaning if that was the case, that was the case.”.

Even after watching the film twice, I am still pleasantly surprised that Artificial actually exists in the world—that Guadagnino was able to capture the man-child bonhomie of coder bros through his fabulous scrim of art film wooziness. I ask Garfield, now a two-time vet of the director’s films, to sum up the full Guadagnino psychedelic experience.

Industry observers note that “Humanity and bodies and interpersonal dynamics and relationship and sexuality, sensuality, Eros, love, the muck and the mire of being human, ambition, drive, greed, power, love, brotherhood, connection,” he says. Guadagnino’s movies are about “his curiosity and love for people: wanting to skin, flay, open up, crack the ribs, and show the insides of these human beings.”.

To Garfield this is the key to understanding the director’s vision for Artificial. Robots didn’t build the robots that might destroy humanity: People did. And people still control them—for now.

Recent findings suggest that artificial inspires a lot of comparisons. Barbaro likens it to Invasion of the Body Snatchers; Garfield compares its climactic confrontation scene to West Side Story. Guadagnino, the actor states, gave another point of reference. Then he does a spot-on, peak-Sicilian impression of the director: “I want this to be like a John Hughes movie.”.

Guadagnino himself is reluctant to name any films that may have inspired this one. But he does name one filmmaker—someone who, as he notes, balanced indie flicks with blockbusters all while building the world’s greatest collection of Haitian art: Jonathan Demme.

It has been revealed that “Jonathan was a humanist, and he had this very profound capacity of eviscerating dynamics of humanism in America,” Guadagnino says. “He did some great movies about the dynamics of corporations versus individual freedom,” like Fighting Mad and Philadelphia.

It has been revealed that barbaro indicates the film’s secret sauce is that it’s up for interpretation. It’s possible to come away from it celebrating the AI bros as heroes or decrying them as villains.

“It’s a bit of a Rorschach test,” she says. “Some people come out shaking, terrified. And I think some people are like, ‘Wow, what a good time!’ I also think that you have to hide the medicine in the food a little bit. I don’t think a purely doomsday story is going to reach many people.”.

UNDER PRESSURE “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film,” Garfield notes. “They didn’t kill it. They could have killed it.”.

Garfield, meanwhile, may leave the film eternally bonded with Altman—the role that could help him finally clinch the Oscar. (Garfield’s been nominated twice but hasn’t won yet.) Before making Artificial, Garfield says, he had a positive impression of Altman. He seemed friendly, “like maybe we would’ve been buddies on the kibbutz.”.

Sources indicate that as he dove deeper, though, Garfield’s feelings about Altman got stranger and more complicated in ways that the film addresses both head-on and obliquely. Is Altman someone who habitually tells tall tales? Uses lies to say what needs to be stated, as Sam tells Ilya in the movie? Imagines anecdotes about waving to the A-lister who’s playing him in a biopic?

In a recent development, whatever Altman’s relationship with reality is, the version of him we see in Artificial is charming, ingratiating, prone to grandiose hallucinations and to telling people exactly what they want to hear—then doing what he was going to do anyway. He’s not far off from an AGI approaching a real human consciousness, art imitating a machine imitating life.

“There are certain threads that feel consistent, which is a questioning of his ability to tell or his commitment to the truth,” Garfield states. “How often is he telling the truth to himself? How often is he telling the truth to others? And how many versions of the truth are there, and how is he utilizing that in order to...”.

“Because I ultimately do believe that Sam feels, in our film and in life, that he is serving the good of mankind.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters. From Bobby Moynihan as your verbose bestie to Weird Al Yankovic as a radio host, there's plenty of star power here--and you can even spot an influential figure from GTA history making a quick cameo. Spoilers below Who could it be now? In one of the later missions, players accompany Boobie on one of his errands. Once they reach a latest club, Boobie meets up with Massive Mike and throws a few jibes at the local help sweeping the floor. That "little Santa" with the broom? None other than Rockstar Games president Sam Houser, who doesn't speak a single word in his brief appearance. As an added touch, Houser's digital doppelganger wears a white t-shirt with the Rockstar Games logo. Because the thumbnail for it is a big ol' spoiler, you can click this link to see the Houser cameo for yourself. This isn't the first time that Houser has cameoed in one of his studio's games. In GTA 3, he voiced one of the Ammu-Nation store clerks, and in GTA: San Andreas, a statue of that Ammu-Nation employee could be found in the game's Downtown Square area. Beyond minor background pedestrian and gangster voice roles in San Andreas and GTA 4, Houser has generally kept a low profile, focusing instead on developing the studio's games. With GTA 6 launching to major critical and commercial success, Houser has also issued a rare statement to mark the occasion. "This is a narrative set in a world of possibilities--and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels and concludes," he noted. Meanwhile, Houser's brother, Dan Houser, is working on an open-world comedy game at Absurd Ventures, the studio he founded after leaving Rockstar Games in 2020. For more on GTA 6, check out GameSpot's Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub for tips, tricks, and walkthroughs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump is reacting to the former leader of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) Elon Musk claiming he’s no longer “MAGA” in the wake of the Republican party’s historic midterm election losses.

According to recent reports, “He’s a friend of mine,” Trump, 80, stated while speaking to NBC News on Thursday, November 19. “What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask — there’s a lot of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.”.

The president continued, “But Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”.

After Musk, 55, spent nearly $500 million on the 2026 midterm elections in an attempt to prop up GOP candidates in various states — only to have the Democratic party turn a number of so-called “red” states blue, including Texas, Mississippi, Alaska and more – the once leader of the infamous DOGE initiative denounced the political movement he once shamelessly championed.

“I mean, I’m not MAGA,” the world’s first trillionaire — who earned more than a reported $200 billion in Trump’s first year of his second term and over $913 billion during year two of the former reality TV star’s second stint in the Oval Office — told The New York Times on Wednesday, November 18, during the outlet’s DealBook Summit.

“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk, who campaigned for Trump during the 2024 presidential election on multiple occasions, continued. “But I, I don’t think I’m, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties.”.

Musk went out to express his regret for spending so much money on what proved to be an ultimately failed effort to prop up the Republican party amid the president’s abysmal approval ratings. (Musk reportedly spent $200 million dollars alone on Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s campaign, only for the scandal-ridden politician to ultimately fall short to Democrat James Talarico.).

Recent findings suggest that “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”.
